Vitamin E | metabolism and requirements


Tissues involved in vitamin E catabolism based on their CYP4F2 expression include the liver and kidney (Hirani et al., 2008),
and intestine (Wang et al., 2007; Uehara et al., 2015). a-Tocopherol catabolism was quantitated using a dual isotope technique. An
intravenous, deuterium-labeled a-tocopherol that was administered as an oil:water emulsion to mimic chylomicrons and a differ-
ently deuterium-labeled a-tocopherol was consumed (Traber et al., 2019b). Remarkably, more than 90% of the catabolism to
urinary a-CEHC took place in the liver when the experimental conditions mimicked normal meal eating. However, when the partic-
ipants fasted for 12 h following the “test” breakfast, both the intestine and liver played equal roles in a-tocopherol catabolism.
These data suggest that delay in intestinal secretion of chylomicrons can markedly increase vitamin E catabolism and thus decrease
bioavailability.
Human vitamin E deﬁciency
The frequency of human vitamin E deﬁciency is very rare. There have been reports of vitamin E deﬁciency symptoms in persons with
protein-calorie malnutrition. Dietary changes such as decreasing fat intakes, substituting fat-free foods for fat-containing ones and
increased reliance of meals away from the home, have resulted in decreased consumption of atocopherol-containing foods.
